opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is just practice. Attacking things is a skill, and like any skill, you get good at it by doing it a lot. The people I know who are really good at breaking systems didn't get there by reading papers about attacks. They got there by sitting down, picking some defense, and trying to break it, over and over again, and getting a feel for where things tend to go wrong.

One thing I've advocated for is treating this a bit more like how the traditional security community trains people. In computer security you have capture-the-flag competitions, wargames, a whole culture of "here's a vulnerable thing, go break it." People spend years doing these exercises before they ever find a real bug in production software. In machine learning we don't really have that pipeline. We tend to go straight from "I read some papers" to "I'm going to write a paper," and you skip the part where you build intuition on problems where the answer is known.

So one concrete thing is to just take published defenses and try to break them. There are a lot of them, and many of them are breakable. Even if you only re-break something someone else already broke, that's a great exercise, because you can check your work against what the experts did. I've put together some material along these lines, collections of defenses with the idea that people should work through them the way you'd work through problem sets in a textbook.

The other thing is mindset. A lot of ML researchers are trained to think in averages: what's the accuracy on the test set, does the loss go down? Attacking requires a different frame. You're not asking whether it works on average. You're asking whether there exists any input, anywhere, that makes it fail. That worst-case thinking doesn't come naturally to most people trained in ML, and I think it's something you have to deliberately cultivate.

And then I'd say there's a cultural piece. Attack papers are sometimes seen as less valuable than defense papers, like you're just tearing down someone else's work. I really disagree with that. We only know a defense works if serious people have tried hard to break it and failed. So I'd like to see the community value attack work more, reward people for doing it carefully, and make it a normal, respected career path rather than a side thing. If you make it something people are excited to do and get credit for, you'll get a lot more people who are good at it.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls practice the most important factor and describes repeatedly trying to break defenses to build skill.

r002.rationale: The candidate says machine learning lacks a training pipeline for attacks, but does not say the field is so young that no researchers who began their PhDs in it have graduated.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, and honestly my answer is a little unsatisfying because I don't think there's a shortcut. The way I learned to break things was by breaking things. Not reading papers about breaking things, actually sitting down with a system and trying to make it do something it wasn't supposed to do, failing for a long time, and eventually noticing something.

So the first thing I'd say is: you have to actually do it. A lot of people want to learn how to attack models by reading the attack literature, and that's useful for knowing what's been done, but it's not how you develop the instinct. The instinct comes from staring at a defense and asking, "Okay, what assumption is this making that I don't believe?" And the only way to get good at that is reps. Pick some defense, ideally a recent one that's been published and claims to work, and try to break it. Most of the time you'll succeed, because most defenses don't work. And the times you don't succeed, you'll learn something real about why.

The second thing, which I think is underrated, is that attacking is fundamentally about adversarial thinking, and that's a mindset more than a skill set. The people I know who are really good at this didn't come from any particular background. Some came from security, some from ML, some from basically nowhere. What they have in common is a kind of stubbornness and a refusal to take claims at face value. When someone says "our model is robust to X," their immediate reaction isn't "great," it's "I bet it isn't, let me check." I don't know how you teach that exactly, but I think you can at least encourage it. In the security community, that skepticism is the default. In ML, the default has historically been to trust the paper. We need to shift that.

Third, I think we need better incentives. Right now if you're a grad student and you spend six months breaking someone's defense, you get maybe a workshop paper and you've annoyed a senior person in the field. If you spend six months proposing a new defense, you get a main conference paper and people are excited. That's backwards. The attack work is often more rigorous and more useful, because a broken defense that everyone believes in is actively harmful. So venues should value this, and senior people should be gracious when their stuff gets broken, because it will get broken, and that's the point.

And then more practically, I'd say the barrier to entry for language models specifically is actually pretty low compared to, say, breaking cryptography or finding kernel bugs. You don't need special hardware, you don't need years of background. You need an API key and some creativity. So I'd tell people to just start. Take a model, try to get it to do something it refuses to do, and when you find something, write it up carefully. Explain what you tried, what worked, what didn't, and why you think it worked. That last part is what separates a cute jailbreak from actual research.

The last thing I'd add is that I think there's a bit of a confusion between "attacking" meaning jailbreaking and "attacking" meaning the broader security research mindset. Jailbreaks are fine, but the more interesting work is things like: can I extract training data, can I steal the model, can I poison it, can I figure out what it's actually computing. Those require more technical depth but they're also where I think the real long-term value is. So I'd encourage people not to stop at "I made the model say a bad word" and keep going toward "I understand something about how this system fails."

r001.rationale: The response says skill comes from actually trying to break systems through repeated practice, learning by failing, and testing defenses directly.

r002.rationale: It does not say that the field is so young that no PhD students who began working on language-model attacks have graduated.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest thing is to make it easy for people to try. Attacking a system is a skill you develop by actually doing it. You come up with an idea, you test it, it doesn’t work, and then you try to understand why. Over time, you build an intuition for where the system might fail.

And language models are interesting because the barrier to getting started is relatively low. You don’t necessarily need a deep background in machine learning to notice that a model behaves strangely and start investigating. But there’s a big difference between finding one amusing failure and doing good research. Can you make the attack reliable? Does it work on other models? Can you explain what assumption the defense made that turned out to be wrong?

So I’d like to see more opportunities for people to work on concrete attack problems, with access to the systems and feedback from people who have experience. And we should reward careful work that breaks things. If all the recognition goes to building a new defense, you’re not going to develop the community of attackers you need to figure out whether those defenses actually work.

r001.rationale: It says attacking is a skill developed by doing it: proposing ideas, testing them, learning from failures, and building intuition.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that the field is so young that no PhD researchers who began in it have graduated.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most important thing is to give people opportunities to actually try attacking models. This is a skill you develop by doing it. You try something, it doesn’t work, and then you have to figure out whether your idea was wrong or whether there’s some detail you haven’t understood yet.

And you need a setting where that feedback is meaningful. If someone finds an attack, can they report it? Can they learn why it worked? Can they see what happens when the defender tries to fix it? That back-and-forth teaches you much more than just collecting examples of a model saying something it shouldn’t.

The other thing I’d encourage is bringing in people from computer security. The habit of looking at a system and asking, ‘What assumption is everyone making here, and what happens if I violate it?’ is very useful. You still have to learn the details of language models, but you don’t necessarily need to start as a machine learning expert to have a good idea for an attack.

So I’d like to see more accessible challenges, more opportunities to work with experienced researchers, and more credit for careful attack work—including work that shows that a proposed defense doesn’t actually solve the problem. If we want people to get good at this, we have to make it a worthwhile thing to spend their time doing.

r001.rationale: The response says attacking models is a skill developed by trying attacks, learning from failures, and refining ideas through feedback.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention the field’s age or that no PhD researchers who began their studies on this topic have graduated.
